inputs.name: atmospheric_density

row_source: Earth-GRAM User Guide, NASA/TM-20210022157 (White & Hoffman, 2021) pp. 63-65: worked example, 3.61% at 0 km. Conditions: 22.0N 48.0E, Julian Day 2458934.02, daily F10.7 = 148, mean F10.7 = 67, Ap = 16.
Same source, same worked example: 4.72% at 40 km.

GRAM-95, NASA-TM-4715 (Justus et al., 1995) Table 3.3 p. 21: OBSERVED density perturbation 4.2% over the 45-65 km band, 10 Shuttle re-entries (Findlay & Jasinski 1990). Table 3.1 p. 19 gives 3.3% observed over 22 re-entries; the larger of the two is used. Plotted here at the band midpoint, 55 km.
GRAM-95, NASA-TM-4715 Table 3.3 p. 21: OBSERVED 5.7% over the 65-85 km band, same 10 re-entries (Table 3.1: 5.1% over 22). Plotted at the band midpoint, 75 km.

ENGINEERING JUDGMENT built on a primary RANGE. U.S. Standard Atmosphere Supplements 1966 (NTRS 19670028571) p. 28: Faire & Champion falling-sphere measurements give a mean +15% above Standard at 90 km with individual maxima +30%. Converting an observed range from 12 measurements into a 1-sigma is the judgment; no source states a sigma above 86 km.
ENGINEERING JUDGMENT on the same primary range. 1966 Supplements p. 28: at 100 km, several percent below to +65% above Standard. Half-width / 2 taken as a 1-sigma proxy.
ENGINEERING JUDGMENT on the same primary range. 1966 Supplements p. 28: at 110 km, -20% to +62% (Nov + Feb mean +36%, individually +13% to +62%; July -15% to +5%).
ENGINEERING JUDGMENT on the same primary range. 1966 Supplements p. 5: at 120 km, January mid-latitude ~+50% above Standard, summer/low-latitude ~-20% below.

ENGINEERING JUDGMENT: the 120 km value HELD to 150 km. Nothing was sourced between 120 and 200 km. GRAM-99 (NASA/TM-1999-209630 section 2.9 p. 14) gives 3.0% at the equator to 8.0% at the poles, but states it for altitudes >= 200 km and it is deliberately NOT extrapolated downwards.

inputs.source: Mixed tier - see `row_source` above, row by row. The 0-85 km rows are T1 standard deviations from NASA's own GRAM validation against Shuttle re-entry data. The >=90 km rows are ENGINEERING JUDGMENT: no document opened in the sourcing pass states a 1-sigma density dispersion above 86 km, so those rows convert primary OBSERVED RANGES (U.S. Standard Atmosphere Supplements 1966, falling-sphere data) into a 1-sigma proxy, which is this project's step and not any source's. The input is tiered T3 overall because its weakest row governs it.
inputs.notes: CROSS-CHECK, not a source for the numbers: the Stardust entry operations analysis (Desai et al., AIAA 2006-6410, p. 5 / fig. 5) states that across its entry profile "density variations between +-5% to +-25% are possible" as a GRAM-95 3-sigma envelope, i.e. 1.7% to 8.3% at 1-sigma. That is consistent with the rows below 86 km and MUCH SMALLER than the rows above it - unsurprising, since an entry profile's dispersion is dominated by where the dynamic pressure is, but it is a real disagreement and it is stated rather than hidden. NRLMSISE-00's published model-vs-data standard deviations (Picone et al., JGR 107(A12) 2002, archive tables) independently indicate roughly 17-36% over 80-120 km, which corroborates the size of the upper rows; those digits came off an OCR'd table and the conversion from log-density units was the reader's, so it is a T2 corroboration and not the source. SECOND-ORDER, STATED NOT MODELLED: one z-score is drawn per trajectory, so the anomaly is perfectly correlated in altitude (A-UQ-ATM-2). Real dispersion has a finite vertical correlation length; perfect correlation is the conservative choice for trajectory-INTEGRATED quantities, which is what the bondline responds to.

inputs.name: vehicle_mass
inputs.source: ENGINEERING JUDGMENT. No source. 2% 1-sigma on as-built mass against its design value is a plausible mass-properties allocation for a small entry capsule, and nothing in this project supports a number. The nominal 350 kg is itself a placeholder (configs/baseline.yaml), so a sourced dispersion about it would be false precision.
inputs.notes: This is the AS-BUILT knowledge of one vehicle's mass, not the 250-450 kg MISSION range in configs/design_space.yaml. That range asks "what payload is this?" and is a design-space axis (A-OPT-2); this asks "how well do we know this vehicle?".

inputs.name: entry_flight_path_angle
inputs.source: ENGINEERING JUDGMENT. No source. 0.1 deg at 3-sigma on delivered entry flight-path angle stands in for de-orbit burn execution and navigation error at the entry interface. The sourcing pass found entry RESULTS with dispersions (Desai & Qualls' Stardust reconstruction publishes a 3-sigma of +-3.64 g on peak deceleration) but no published dispersion on the delivered angle itself, which is what this input is.
inputs.notes: The M4 design space treats flight-path angle as a DESIGN variable over [-8.0, -1.5] deg. This input is the error about whichever value the design picked, and it is applied as an OFFSET for that reason.

inputs.name: effective_nose_radius_model
inputs.source: NASA TN D-5121 (Ellison, 1969) p. 5, verbatim: "The data of the present investigation agree with the results of Zoby and Sullivan (ref. 6) within 10 percent for K = 0 and K = 0.707; however, for K = 0.417 and R = 0, the disagreement is about 20 percent." Both documents are primary and both were opened (docs/validation/sourcing_report.md item 8). T1.
inputs.notes: THE DOMINANT HEATING UNCERTAINTY, and the reason M7 exists in the form it does. R_eff enters Sutton-Graves as 1/sqrt(R_eff), so the sources' own ~20% disagreement at K ~ 0.42 - exactly where the M4 front sits - is about +-10% on heat flux, against the correlation constant's own +-4%. It is a DISCRETE switch and not a Gaussian because that is what the evidence is: two reports, one of which is closer to right, and no continuum between them. The 50/50 split is declared INDIFFERENCE between two primaries, not a measured frequency; a reader who trusts Ellison more should re-run with the probabilities changed here and the report will say so. See A-UQ-NOSE-1 for the three ways the alternative state is WIDER than what Ellison's sentence strictly licenses.

inputs.name: sutton_graves_coefficient
inputs.source: NASA TR R-376 (Sutton & Graves, 1971) Table II p. 39, read off a 300 dpi render: the correlation's own fit error for air is 3.3% average, 9.8% maximum. ASSUMPTIONS A-HEAT-1 and docs/negative_results.md NR-12 declare that this project therefore treats the correlation as +-4% AT BEST and propagates that here. T1.
inputs.notes: +-4% sits between the primary's AVERAGE (3.3%) and MAXIMUM (9.8%) fit errors and is the project's declared reading, not a number printed anywhere. A worst-case study should widen this to [0.902, 1.098] and say it did. It is uniform, not normal: a fit-error bound is a band, and a band is not a standard deviation. This covers the CONSTANT only. The model FORM - catalycity, hot wall, radiation - is gate G2', which is LIMITED and untouched, and where catalycity alone is worth about a factor of two (A-HEAT-2..4). Nothing here propagates that.

inputs.name: high_altitude_heating_model
inputs.source: ENGINEERING JUDGMENT on the size; the NEED for the term is measured. docs/negative_results.md NR-14 records that 5-20% of a feasible design's integrated heat load - and hence its bondline temperature - accrues above 86 km, where the atmosphere is a log-interpolated transcribed table (gate G1A', LIMITED above the five primary-checked rows) and where the flow is transitional to rarefied, which a continuum stagnation-point correlation does not describe. No source quantifies how wrong Sutton-Graves is there, so the +-50% band is judgment.
inputs.notes: Multiplies the HEAT FLUX above 86 km only, not the density, so it does not perturb drag in that band - the atmospheric_density input does that, and the two are separate questions (A-UQ-HI86-1). DIRECTION: the physical argument points DOWNWARD - continuum correlations over-predict as Knudsen number rises and rarefied bridging functions reduce stagnation heating - so a symmetric band is probably conservative on the high side. That argument is UNSOURCED here and the band is left symmetric rather than skewed on an unsupported mechanism.

inputs.name: tps_conductivity
inputs.source: ENGINEERING JUDGMENT. ASSUMPTIONS A-TPS-7 states that the stack's properties are engineering placeholders "of the right order for a low-density insulator", not the properties of any qualified TPS material. So the uncertainty here is not batch variability of a known material - it is not knowing which material this is - and no source can be cited for a spread about a placeholder.
inputs.notes: EPISTEMIC, not aleatory, for that reason: the number does not change between flights, it is simply unknown. The insulator only. The second layer is aluminium-like structure whose conductivity (150 W/mK) is known to far better than this and is not perturbed. A-TPS-2 additionally holds k temperature-INDEPENDENT, and notes that a real insulator's k rises with temperature, which would raise bondline temperature in the long shallow case. That is a separate, unmodelled model-form error; this input does not stand in for it.

inputs.name: tps_specific_heat
inputs.source: ENGINEERING JUDGMENT, for the same reason as tps_conductivity (A-TPS-7 placeholder properties). Narrower than the conductivity band because specific heat varies less between low-density insulators than conductivity does - which is itself a judgment.

inputs.name: cd_surrogate_gp
inputs.source: Measured at surface build time and stored in data/aero/cfd_surface_v2/surface.json: the GP predictive standard deviation of C_D,fore at this shape, WIDENED by the k-fold cross-validation z-score spread (the stored `sigma_inflation` - read from that file, not repeated here) because cross-validation showed the raw GP to be overconfident. T1 in the sense that it is this project's own measurement on its own data, reproducible from the persisted surface.
inputs.notes: ONE draw per trajectory, not per time step: the surface error is a smooth function of Mach for one shape, not white noise (A-AERO-2). Skipped at Fidelity 0, where there is no surrogate for it to be about.

inputs.name: cd_discretisation
inputs.source: results/M2/<run>/gci.csv, read at call time and never typed (aerodynamics.cfd_surface.discretisation_band). For the coarse level the band is 1.25 x the Richardson error estimate of the coarse mesh (Celik et al. 2008 safety factor). T1 as a measurement of this project's own mesh study - once that study exists.
inputs.notes: THIS WAS THE REFUSAL, and still is if the file goes away: while M2's GCI table was empty (gate G4 IN_PROGRESS) a run that selected the CFD drag surface STOPPED here rather than quietly propagate one fewer C_D term (A-CFD-9). Since run M2-20260920T123901Z the table exists (G4 PASS, NR-25) and the hook returns the coarse-level band from it - plus the file's LABELLED iterative columns (residual limit-cycle half-amplitude), under their own names; what is sampled is the file's combined discretisation + iterative value. Nothing is typed: delete gci.csv and this input refuses again. A-CFD-9 also records that a SPHERE's GCI is not a capsule's - so the term is a transfer, not a measurement of the surface itself.

inputs.name: cd_perfect_gas_model_form
inputs.source: ENGINEERING JUDGMENT, declared as such by the model it belongs to. A-CFD-12 carries a "+-5% model-form half-band that is NOT validated here" for using calorically perfect air (gamma = 1.4, A-CFD-1) at shock-layer conditions where it is wrong. The argument for it is from theory (stagnation Cp ~ 1.84 at gamma = 1.4 against the Newtonian limit 2.0); no measurement supports the 5%.
inputs.notes: The half-band itself lives in the surface's metadata as `model_form_rel_halfband`; this input only draws the POSITION within it, uniformly, because it is a band.

inputs.name: cd_base_drag
inputs.source: NASA TN D-4800 (Miller, 1968; NTRS 19680026196) fig. 11(b), opened and read for M3: area-mean base-pressure ratio p_b/p_inf for blunted 9-deg cones at Mach 10-20 lies between about 0.2 and about 3. Those end values were READ OFF A LOG-SCALE GRAPH BY EYE and are good to perhaps +-30%, which is why they set the WIDTH of a band and nothing else. The lower end, p_b = 0, is the exact vacuum limit.
inputs.notes: Sampled UNIFORMLY, as src/aether/aerodynamics/base_drag.py instructs in as many words: "a band is not a standard deviation". No flight-Reynolds-number source was found (sourcing report item 4, unresolved gap); the Mars 2020 MEDLI2 backshell paper would close it and is paywalled.

comparison.tpi_footnote: The Thermal Penetration Index column is reported FOR COMPLETENESS ONLY. Spec §44 asked for it; the §44 study (`reports/milestones/TPI_study.md`, `docs/negative_results.md` NR-10) returned the verdict **DISCARD**: over the M1b design grid, TPI's ranking of designs is 99.94% reconstructible by rank regression on (peak bondline temperature, integrated heat load), its Spearman correlation with peak bondline temperature alone is +0.9992, and a TPI-minimising optimiser selects the same design as a bondline-minimising one. All 16 declared combinations of reference temperature and weighting family failed the pre-declared redundancy criterion, so it is not an artefact of one setting. The mechanism is shape invariance: every design produces very nearly the same normalised depth profile, so any weighted depth integral of it recovers the scale factor and nothing more. It is printed here so a reader can check that claim on these four designs rather than take it on trust, and it is NOT used to rank anything.
